answers.explanation: Forward lookups are by far the most common: every web page, email, and app connection starts with one.
One small question and one small answer: UDP skips the handshake, and the client simply retries if nothing comes back. Port 67 is DHCP and 25 is mail.
Zone transfers and answers too large for one UDP packet use TCP, still on port 53.
One file at one site couldn't keep up with a fast-growing network. DNS spreads the database across many servers.
DNS runs at the application layer, on top of UDP. It acts like infrastructure because nearly every other application needs it.
If you can reach an IP address but no name works, the names aren't being resolved. Pinging an address skips DNS entirely.
gethostbyaddr takes an address and looks for a record under in-addr.arpa. gethostbyname goes the other way.
/etc/hosts maps names to addresses locally. Attackers like it too: one line there can quietly redirect a bank's name.
